info.title: Kotlin vs Rust for GraalVM native compile

parts.text: I am thinking if it would be better to implement the protocol and html renderer in kotlin or java instead of embedding rust crates? Does it make a difference for native compile via graalvm?

The user is asking a design/architecture question: would it be better to implement the protocol and HTML renderer in Kotlin/Java instead of embedding Rust crates, and does it make a difference for native compile via GraalVM.

This is a research/analysis question in plan mode. I need to read the codebase to understand current architecture—particularly `pathland-render-html` in Rust and its JVM JNA shim, and how the Rust core is consumed. Then analyze GraalVM native-image implications.

Let me investigate the relevant files: the Java `pathland-render-html` JNA shim, the Rust render-html crate, the Kotlin protocol implementation (pathland-view-core has a hand-written JVM protocol mirror already!), and how the Rust dylibs are embedded.

Key facts from AGENTS.md:
- `pathland-view-core` Kotlin already owns a hand-written protocol mirror (wire codec, ring, etc.) — the JVM side already implements the protocol in Kotlin! Only the HTML renderer is Rust (pathland-render-html) consumed via JNA.
- Rust crates embed dylibs in jars via META-INF/native.
- GraalVM native-image: JNA with dylib loading works but requires resources config; native-image has FFI support.

Let me look at actual code to give a grounded answer. Let me explore.

I should do parallel searches. Let me look at lib/java/pathland-render-html and lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html, and the JVM protocol implementation.
I'll investigate the current split between Rust and JVM code before weighing in.

# pathland-render-html (Java) — implementation status

**Last updated:** October 28, 2026

The **Java binding to the Rust HTML renderer** (`dev.pathland.render.html`) — a
thin **JNA shim** over `libpathland_render_html`. There is a **single renderer**
(the Rust crate), reused by every language; the former hand-written retained
Java renderer is removed. Protocol contract: `spec/`.

## Implemented

- **Stateless JNA shim**: `HtmlRenderer.instance()` links the Rust cdylib;
  `render(frame, root)` / `renderFragment(frame, root)` /
  `renderFullSnapshot(frame, root)` render a self-contained snapshot frame to
  HTML in one pass (no retained tree, no `applyFrame`); `pathland_html_free`
  releases native strings. Lazy-loaded; skipped (test assumption) when the dylib
  is absent from `java.library.path`.
- **Debug comments**: `renderDebug(frame, root)` / `renderFragmentDebug(...)`
  bind the Rust `pathland_html_render_debug` exports — each rendered node is
  prefixed with an HTML comment naming its component type and the modifiers
  applied (opt-in; the plain `render` output is unchanged).
- **Full Rust renderer surface** (canonical): all spec components render inline
  (structural + decorative CSS in a single `style` attribute), ARIA/event
  attributes, `IS_SECURE` → password, `TOGGLE_STYLE` variants,
  `DATE_PICKER_MODE`, and literal colors inline. The default `render(...)`
  injects the renderer's built-in `<style>` block (preflight reset + design
  tokens + `.pathland-*` component defaults) into every document — no
  `/tailwind.css`. `renderLinked(frame, root, cssBase)` /
  `renderLinkedDebug(...)` instead emit a content-hashed
  `<link rel="stylesheet" href="{cssBase}/{baseCssName()}">`; token overrides
  and fit-band rules stay inline. `baseCss()` / `baseCssName()` bind the Rust
  `pathland_html_base_css[_name]` exports so the Spring/Quarkus starters serve
  the renderer-owned bytes immutable. A missing linked export degrades to the
  inline document.
- **Icon glyphs from the shared renderer**: `iconSvg(String name)` binds the
  Rust `pathland_html_icon_svg` export over the C ABI — the full inline `<svg>`
  for a canonical `ICON_NAME` (unknown/extension names → the renderer's
  fallback glyph, never null). Hosts serve `/_pathland/icons/<name>.svg` from
  it (Spring/Quarkus route a few lines in their starters), so the DOM client's
  lazy icon fetch gets the same glyph data SSR inlines from — one Rust source,
  no per-platform static icon files. `HtmlRendererTest` covers it.
- **Demos use the shim**: `SessionApp` no longer calls `applyFrame`; SSR renders
  the mount frame through `HtmlRenderer.render(sink.frame(), rootId)`. The
  renderer is compiled once at startup.
- **Text fields share one component class**: `TEXT_FIELD` inputs and `TEXT_EDITOR`
  textareas render with `class="pathland-input"` (Tailwind-style inset-outline
  styling from the Rust renderer's CSS); the copied `@pathland/dom-renderer`
  bundle (content-hashed `dom-renderer-<sha256>.js` in both demos) mirrors the
  class so delta-created fields hydrate identically.

## Removed (September 2026)

- `compileTailwind(overrideCss)` and the `pathland_tailwind_compile` binding are
  **deleted** — the renderer is inline-only now and needs no compiler. The demo
  `/tailwind.css` endpoints (`TailwindCssController` / `TailwindCssResource`)
  and the `<link rel="stylesheet" href="/tailwind.css">` in both `SessionApp`
  files are removed.

## Not implemented / gaps

- **Typography uses the platform system font stack** (`system-ui,
  -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, …`) — the Rust renderer's document head
  makes no external/webfont requests, so the demo pages render without loading
  any font files and work offline. An app can still override `font.body.family`
  via a `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` to any font it hosts.
- The shim is unaffected by the Rust renderer's September 2026 shell alignment
  (SPACER/MENU/STEPPER/GAUGE/PICKER markup now matches the DOM client's runtime
  shells); the demos' SSR output reflects the Rust renderer as-is, pinned by the
  `pathland-html-golden` conformance harness. `HtmlRendererTest` covers the
  semantic-role → element mapping (`NAVIGATION`→`<nav>`, `HEADER`→`<h2>`,
  `TEXT_STYLE` headings) and the DSL's rejection of non-semantic role codes,
  plus media rendering (a `VIDEO` surface bound to its `MEDIA_CONTROLLER` —
  native `<video controls>` + `data-pathland-controller`, the non-visual hidden
  controller shell, image `alt` from the accessibility label,
  `ContentMode Fill`→`cover`).

## Verified by

`mvn test -pl pathland-render-html` — JNA shim tests (skip when the Rust dylib
is absent), including the linked stylesheet link + `baseCss`/`baseCssName`
exposure; part of the non-demo reactor run on JDK 17.

---
# pathland-render-html

The HTML renderer: a stateless, streaming pure function of the opcode stream
that maps declarative frames onto HTML elements — Pathland's server-side /
remote-projection target.

Part of [Pathland](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland). Depends on
[`pathland-core`](https://crates.io/crates/pathland-core) and
[`pathland-core-transport`](https://crates.io/crates/pathland-core-transport).

## License

Apache-2.0.

  -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, …`) — the Rust renderer's document head
  makes no external/webfont requests, so the demo pages render without loading
  any font files and work offline. An app can still override `font.body.family`
  via a `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` to any font it hosts.
- The shim is unaffected by the Rust renderer's September 2026 shell alignment
  (SPACER/MENU/STEPPER/GAUGE/PICKER markup now matches the DOM client's runtime
  shells); the demos' SSR output reflects the Rust renderer as-is, pinned by the
  `pathland-html-golden` conformance harness. `HtmlRendererTest` covers the
  semantic-role → element mapping (`NAVIGATION`→`<nav>`, `HEADER`→`<h2>`,
  `TEXT_STYLE` headings) and the DSL's rejection of non-semantic role codes,
  plus media rendering (a `VIDEO` surface bound to its `MEDIA_CONTROLLER` —
  native `<video controls>` + `data-pathland-controller`, the non-visual hidden
  controller shell, image `alt` from the accessibility label,
  `ContentMode Fill`→`cover`).

`mvn test -pl pathland-render-html` — JNA shim tests (skip when the Rust dylib
is absent), including the linked stylesheet link + `baseCss`/`baseCssName`
exposure; part of the non-demo reactor run on JDK 17.

# pathland-render-html

The HTML renderer: a stateless, streaming pure function of the opcode stream
that maps declarative frames onto HTML elements — Pathland's server-side /
remote-projection target.

Part of [Pathland](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland). Depends on
[`pathland-core`](https://crates.io/crates/pathland-core) and
[`pathland-core-transport`](https://crates.io/crates/pathland-core-transport).

Now let's understand the prior Java renderer history — it was removed. Let me find that commit and its rationale. Search git log for "retained Java renderer" or deletions.

Let me look at the commit removing the Java renderer, and whether native-image is used anywhere in build scripts/CI.

Also important for GraalVM: the current Java stack uses JNA to load dylibs embedded in jars. Under GraalVM native-image, that dylib still needs to be present at runtime (native-image doesn't embed/extract the jar resource unless configured via `-H:IncludeResources`; JNA's `Native.load` with an absolute path works, but the `extractEmbedded` mechanism relies on classpath resources and `getResourceAsStream`; in native-image resources must be registered). Also JNA itself works on native-image with some config (JNA is supported; `com.sun.jna` has feature? Actually native-image supports JNA since GraalVM 21+ with `--initialize-at-build-time` etc.). But the commons issue: JNA's `Native.load` by name requires the library available at runtime; shipping a native image doesn't bundle the dylib.

If protocol + HTML renderer were pure Kotlin/Java, then GraalVM native-image could compile everything ahead-of-time into a single static-ish executable: no JNA, no dylib extraction, no JNI. That's a real benefit. Downside: duplicate implementation, divergence risk, maintenance, and the Rust renderer is 4.7k lines with golden tests; Kotlin implementation would need to be rebuilt and kept byte-identical? Actually HTML string output must match the DOM client and golden tests.

Let me quantify: The Rust HTML renderer is ~6k lines including debug/tokens. The JVM protocol is already implemented in Kotlin (FrameCodec, Opcode, all constants). So the "protocol in Java" question is basically already answered: it IS in Kotlin. But the Rust core remains canonical for Rust/GTK/Qt demo.

I have a good picture. Let me also check the JS DOM renderer size to understand the duplication (SSR Rust + TS client). And check whether there's a golden conformance harness comparing Rust HTML output (pathland-html-golden). This matters: if implementing in Kotlin, you'd need to match same golden output. Also check the Maven module list and release build for native images.

Let me check the size of the TS DOM renderer and the golden test harness, plus git history rationale for choosing Rust (the AGENTS.md already says "one renderer, every language"). The decision was deliberate.

Let me also think about GraalVM native-image specifics for the answer:

Current architecture:
- JVM protocol/engine already pure Kotlin (no native).
- JVM server uses `libpathland_render_html` via JNA, jar embeds per-platform dylibs.
- Markdown parser: JVM `dev.pathland.markdown.Markdown` uses JNA to `libpathland_markdown` per the grep. Wait — AGENTS said JVM has embedded inline-Markdown parser in Kotlin, but the Java file says it's a JNA shim over libpathland_markdown. Let me verify. The grep shows Markdown.java with JNA binding to `libpathland_markdown`. So both HTML renderer and Markdown are native on the JVM path.

So for GraalVM native-image:
1. Native-image AOT compiles the JVM code. JNA is supported but requires configuration; JNA's dynamic proxy/interface mapping relies on reflection and `Native.load`. GraalVM supports JNA (since 21.x) with `--enable-native-access` and needs `jna` feature; but dynamic library loading by absolute path at runtime works. However the embedded dylib extraction uses jar resources: native-image does not include classpath resources unless registered via `-H:IncludeResources=...`. So `getResourceAsStream("/META-INF/native/...")` returns null in a native image unless resources are registered. You'd need resource-config or `-H:IncludeResources`.
2. Even if resource extraction works, you'd ship a native executable + a separate dylib file (or extract it to temp at runtime). That's awkward but doable.
3. JNA on native-image: GraalVM's `native-image` supports JNA via the `jna` feature? Actually, GraalVM has support for JNI and "Foreign Function & Memory API" (FFM), and there's special support for JNA: `com.sun.jna` requires `--initialize-at-build-time`? Let me recall. There is a well-known issue: JNA in native-image is supported since GraalVM 22.2? There are community configs. JNA registers its callbacks etc. It's generally possible but has friction. Alternatively, use Panama FFM (Java 22+; but project supports Java 17, so FFM is preview on 17-21). JNA is the pragmatic choice.
4. If HTML renderer were pure Kotlin/Java, native-image would make it fully self-contained: no CDylib files, no per-platform artifacts, no extraction, no JNA. That is a significant operational win for GraalVM deployments (single executable, smaller container). Quarkus native is a big use case.
5. But the cost: reimplement ~6k lines of Rust HTML renderer in Kotlin, keep byte-identical output (golden tests, DOM client hydration contract), and maintain two implementations or drop Rust server-side? Note the Rust HTML renderer is also used by Rust/other hosts? Actually `pathland-render-html` is a Rust crate that could be used by Rust SSR (but Rust demos don't SSR; the server is JVM). Is the Rust HTML renderer used by anything besides JVM? The architecture says "one renderer, every language" — Swift/.NET via C ABI. If you move to Kotlin, you lose cross-language reuse unless you also port. That's the core tradeoff.

Alternative middle ground: keep Rust renderer for non-JVM; add a pure-Java renderer for JVM, and a conformance suite that asserts both produce identical HTML for golden frames. This preserves GraalVM friendliness while avoiding drift via the golden harness. But that's two implementations to maintain.

Another option: use GraalVM native-image with JNA properly configured (resources + JNA config) and extract the dylib; keep single Rust renderer. Or ship the dylib alongside the native executable and set `pathland.render.html.lib` to a path — no resource extraction needed. Under native-image you can set `-Dpathland.render.html.lib=/app/libpathland_render_html.so`. That's the least-effort path if the goal is just GraalVM.

Important: GraalVM native images for the *server* also need JNA for the protocol? No — protocol is pure Kotlin. Only render-html and markdown use JNA on the server. Wait, `PathlandCore` JNA ring is only used by desktop demos, not server. So only 2 native deps on server: render-html and markdown.

Markdown could be ported to Kotlin too (there's a Java `Markdown` but it's a JNA shim, not pure).

Also worth noting: GraalVM native-image doesn't run in interpreted JIT mode; the Rust dylib is still native anyway, so runtime performance is fine. The main issue is packaging/portability, not performance.

Another angle: Quarkus native + JNA. Quarkus supports native with JNA? Quarkus's native image build would need `quarkus.native.additional-build-args=-H:IncludeResources=...` and JNA substitutions. This can be fragile. Pure JVM renderer would make Quarkus native trivial.

Also: If implementing in Java/Kotlin, the HTML renderer is a pure function of the frame, so it's straightforward to port and test against golden output. The Rust code is 4689 lines in lib.rs + debug 451 + token/role/icon/css ~500 = ~5.9k. A Kotlin port is maybe 4-5k lines. Not trivial but feasible.

But there's a strategic principle in AGENTS.md: "one renderer, every language" and "protocol is king". They deliberately removed the Java renderer (commit e9aade28) to avoid divergence. So recommending a reversal needs a strong reason. The strongest reason is GraalVM native.

Does it actually make a difference for native compile via GraalVM? Yes:
- With Rust dylib via JNA: native-image needs JNA configuration and resource inclusion; the output is not single-file (must ship .so/.dylib and extract or point at it); cross-platform native build needs the matching Rust dylib per target; `System.load`/JNA works but adds startup work.
- Pure Kotlin/Java: fully AOT-compiled, single executable, no JNA, no embedded natives, no extraction, ideally smaller image and less config. Also `native-image` can close-world optimize the renderer.

However, there's a caveat: GraalVM native-image can't close-world optimize across JNI/JNA anyway; JNA is a runtime dependency. And shipping multi-arch native images already requires per-arch builds, so shipping a per-arch .so alongside is not much extra burden. But the classic "distroless single binary" story is worse.

Let me verify whether Quarkus/Spring native is actually a goal in the repo (any docs mention GraalVM support). Search docs/spec.

# their Rust cdylibs, and the demo module needs the Java reactor sources:
#
#   docker build -f lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/Dockerfile -t pathland-quarkus-demo .
#
# See docs/DEPLOY.md.

# --- Stage 1: the Rust HTML renderer + inline-Markdown cdylibs (embedded into jars) ---
FROM rust:1-slim AS rust
WORKDIR /src
COPY lib/rust ./lib/rust
RUN cargo build --manifest-path lib/rust/Cargo.toml \
    -p pathland-render-html -p pathland-markdown-capi

# --- Stage 2: the Java reactor + the Quarkus app (jars embed the dylibs) ---
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17 AS java
WORKDIR /src
COPY --from=rust /src/lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_render_html.so \
     lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_render_html.so
COPY --from=rust /src/lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_markdown.so \
     lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_markdown.so
COPY lib/java ./lib/java
# Include the extension's deployment module in the reactor: the runtime module's
# quarkus-extension-maven-plugin validates its dependencies against it, and it is
# not a Maven dependency of the demo (so -am alone would omit it).
RUN mvn -q -B -f lib/java/pom.xml \
    -pl pathland-quarkus-demo,pathland-quarkus-deployment \
    -am package -Dmaven.test.skip=true

# --- Stage 3: runtime (JRE only) ---
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=java /src/lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/target/quarkus-app/ /app/
EXPOSE 8080
ENV QUARKUS_HTTP_PORT=8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-Xms64m", "-Xmx256m", "-jar", "/app/quarkus-run.jar"]---

parts.text:
I now have enough to answer. The user asks a question, so I should give a well-grounded analysis and recommendation, not implement. Plan mode requires a plan though — but the task is advisory. I should present the analysis, tradeoffs, and a proposed plan/options, and ask which they want.

Let me quantify the actual native surface on the JVM server path:
- `pathland-view-core` protocol/engine: pure Kotlin. No Rust needed (JNA Ring interop is optional/lazy, used only desktop). Wait — `PathlandCore.kt` JNA is in pathland-view-core and lazily loaded; but for server don't call it. So no Rust.
- `dev.pathland.render.html`: Rust dylib via JNA (HTML renderer ~5.9k LOC).
- `dev.pathland.markdown.Markdown`: Rust dylib via JNA (pathland-markdown-capi). Hmm, but AGENTS.md says JVM has embedded inline-Markdown parser in Kotlin. Let me verify: Markdown.java in main/java uses JNA. But maybe there's also a Kotlin parser `dev.pathland.markdown.Markdown`? The grep found only the Java file. So AGENTS is slightly inaccurate or paths list "embedded inline-Markdown parser" but actually native. Let me quickly confirm markdown size.

Anyway, the key answer:

1. Protocol on JVM is already Kotlin. So "implement protocol in Kotlin" is already done — no action.
2. HTML renderer is the only substantial Rust-native dependency (plus Markdown).
3. GraalVM native-image impact: real but modest, and depends on deployment approach.

GraalVM specifics:
- JNA is supported by GraalVM native-image (since 22.2ish), but requires reachability metadata. JNA's own metadata ships with JNA 5.14 (has `META-INF/native-image/.../jna` config? JNA 5.13+ includes native-image metadata). Let me recall: JNA added GraalVM native-image support in 5.9; it has `com.sun.jna` feature via `native-image.properties`? Actually JNA provides `META-INF/native-image/com.sun.jna/jna/native-image.properties`. Yes, JNA ships GraalVM metadata since 5.0-ish. So JNA itself works.
- The blockers are (a) resource extraction: `getResourceAsStream("/META-INF/native/...")` needs `-H:IncludeResources=META-INF/native/.*` or resource-config (Quarkus has `quarkus.native.resources.includes`); (b) native-image doesn't ship the dylib automatically — you must include it as a resource and extract to temp (works if resource registered) or ship it beside the executable; (c) cross-compilation: you build the native image on each target OS/arch anyway, so you already have the matching dylib available at build time; (d) `Native.load(absolutePath)` is a runtime dlopen — works in native image; (e) memory/startup: no real difference.
- So with Rust: Quarkus native build needs `quarkus.native.resources.includes=META-INF/native/**` plus JNA reachability metadata, and the resulting native executable extracts the .so to /tmp at startup. That works but is fragile and adds a temp-file dependency (some hardened/read-only containers with noexec /tmp break it). Shipping the .so next to the binary + `-Dpathland.render.html.lib` avoids extraction but breaks the "single binary" property.
- Pure Kotlin/Java: native-image compiles the renderer into the executable. No JNA, no dlopen, no resource extraction, no /tmp, no per-platform .so embedding. One executable. Also Quarkus/Spring native is a first-class, well-trodden path. This is the concrete benefit.

Costs:
- Port ~5.9k lines Rust to Kotlin, keep output byte-identical to the Rust SSR canonical output, because the TS DOM client + golden fixtures assert equality. Best approach: use `pathland-html-golden` fixtures as the acceptance suite; add Kotlin golden test that renders all fixtures and compares exactly. This is actually feasible because the renderer is a pure function.
- Divergence/maintenance: two renderers (Rust for non-JVM hosts; Kotlin for JVM). Mitigate with the golden harness. But AGENTS explicitly rejected this before (removed Java renderer in e9aade28, "single renderer reused by every language").
- The React/DOM client is already a second implementation in TS, so "two implementations" already exists for the DOM side; the golden harness already handles cross-renderer conformance. Adding a Kotlin SSR renderer is a third, but it can be held to the same fixtures.
- Feature velocity: every new opcode/component must be implemented twice (Rust renderer for other hosts + Kotlin). But note: for the server-side story, only the Kotlin one matters; the Rust HTML renderer is only used by the JVM via JNA today. Is it used by any non-JVM host? Not in this repo. So you could move the canonical server renderer to Kotlin and keep the Rust crate for cross-language/embedded/remote projection. Or deprecate the Rust one? That would break the "one renderer every language / Swift .NET via C ABI" architecture.

Middle options:
A. Keep Rust, add proper GraalVM support: resource includes + JNA metadata + a `pathland.render.html.lib` override, and ship the .so in the native image container. Minimal work, preserves single-renderer. Best if GraalVM isn't a top priority and you can ship a sidecar lib.
B. Port HTML renderer (+ Markdown parser) to Kotlin/Java, make the JVM path pure, keep Rust for non-JVM. Add golden conformance so the two can't drift. Best if GraalVM single-binary/Quarkus-native is important.
C. Full port and make Kotlin canonical even for Rust hosts via... no, Rust can't consume JVM. Not viable for the cross-language story.
D. Hybrid: Kotlin renderer only compiled when native profile active, Rust otherwise — avoid, two code paths.

Also worth noting: Markdown is also a native dep; if going pure-JVM for GraalVM, port that too (it's small: pathland-markdown ~? lines). Let me check the markdown crate size quickly. Also pathway `pathland-core-capi` JNA ring is desktop-only, not server; GraalVM native for desktop doesn't make sense.

I should also mention: native-image and JNA "works today" for the desktop? Not relevant.

Another subtle GraalVM point: GraalVM native-image with Kotlin code uses reflection for Kotlin metadata minimally; no issue. Quarkus extension could embed the renderer as plain Kotlin classes.

Also: if they keep Rust, native-image supports JNA but the `Native.load` interface uses dynamic proxies; JNA needs `--enable-native-access` on newer JDKs (JDK 24+) and reflect config for the interface. JNA 5.14 ships native-image metadata; but the `NativeRenderHtml` interface mapping is a JNA `Library` proxy — JNA uses reflection on the interface methods; native-image needs the interface registered. This can be handled with `@AutomaticFeature`/`--initialize-at-build-time` or JNA's `Library.OPTION_...`. Practically there is friction; not zero-config.

Let me verify JNA's GraalVM support level and whether native-image handles it out of the box. I know JNA 5.x includes GraalVM metadata. But the dynamically loaded native library cannot be bundled. So the crux is packaging.

Let me also check the release flow: they ship per-platform dylibs in the jar already (4 platforms). So GraalVM native release would add per-platform .so anyway; that's consistent with current release matrix. But the "native image" benefit (single file) is undercut by shipping a sidecar.

Actually, there's a neat approach for Rust + native-image: statically link Rust into the native image? Not possible directly; native-image links C code via `-H:CLibraryPath` / `--native-link`? Not for arbitrary JNA calls. You can't statically embed a dylib into a GraalVM native image without a C entry/feature. So sidecar or extraction.

Could also consider rewriting the HTML renderer in Kotlin and using it as the canonical implementation, then generating/keeping the Rust one via porting when needed. But the HTML renderer must match DOM client; the golden fixtures provide drift protection. Actually the canonical source of truth is the Rust implementation today (fixtures generated by it). If Kotlin becomes canonical, regenerate fixtures from Kotlin. Cross-language: other hosts needing HTML (Swift/.NET) would lose the renderer unless they reimplement; but the protocol supports network projection: non-JVM hosts could call a server. Hmm.

Let me check the markdown crate size for completeness, then produce the answer.

I should be concise but this is a detailed architecture question; user asked "would it be better" and "does it make a difference for native compile". A structured but not overly long answer. Plan mode: I should present findings/options and ask which direction. I should not make changes.

The JVM server path only pulls in **two** Rust dylibs through JNA:

- `libpathland_render_html` (`pathland-render-html`, ~5.9k LOC) — the real question
- `libpathland_markdown` (`pathland-markdown`, ~520 LOC)

So this is not "Rust protocol vs Kotlin protocol"; it's "keep the SSR HTML renderer in Rust, or reimplement it in Kotlin." The renderer is a pure function of the frame and depends only on `pathland-core`/`pathland-core-transport`, so a port is mechanically feasible.

## Does GraalVM care? Yes — mainly packaging, not speed

Today nothing targets native-image: CI is JVM-only and the Quarkus `Dockerfile` ships a JRE + jars. If you add Quarkus/Spring native later:

- **JNA itself works** under `native-image` (JNA 5.14 ships metadata), but it is not zero-config: reachability/reflection for the `Library` interface plus resource registration for the embedded dylib.
- The jar-extraction path (`getResourceAsStream("/META-INF/native/...")` → temp dir) needs `quarkus.native.resources.includes=META-INF/native/**`, and breaks in hardened containers with read-only/noexec `/tmp`.
- Avoiding extraction means shipping the `.so`/`.dylib` beside the executable and setting `-Dpathland.render.html.lib=...` — which forfeits the "single binary" benefit native images are for.
- A **pure Kotlin renderer** AOT-compiles in: no JNA, no dlopen, no resource extraction, no sidecar lib, one executable. That is a genuine operational difference.
- Runtime performance is a wash (the Rust code is already native); only minor JNA startup/init differs.

## Tradeoffs of porting

- Output must stay **byte-identical**: `lib/rust/crates/pathland-html-golden` treats Rust SSR as canonical and the TS DOM client asserts the same fixtures. A Kotlin port needs a golden test against those fixtures before it can be trusted.
- It creates a second SSR implementation. The repo deliberately removed the Java renderer (`e9aade28`) for a "single renderer, every language" story. The Rust crate is still the cross-language/C-ABI projection target for non-JVM hosts.
- Feature velocity: every new component/property must land in both renderers (mitigated by the golden harness — the TS client already proves cross-renderer drift is testable).

## Recommendation

- **If GraalVM native is on the roadmap now:** port `pathland-render-html` to Kotlin in the JVM module, keep the Rust crate for non-JVM hosts, and wire `pathland-html-golden` into both (port `pathland-markdown` too — it's tiny). This gives you true single-binary native images.
- **If native is speculative:** don't port. Keep the one Rust renderer and add native-image config only when needed (resource include + `pathland.render.html.lib` sidecar). Porting now is a large change for no current deployment gain.
- The protocol should stay where it is (Kotlin on the JVM, Rust canonical for non-JVM); there is no benefit to moving that.

## Recommended direction

Port the **HTML renderer** and the **Markdown parser** to the JVM, keep the Rust renderers for Rust/non-JVM hosts, and make the existing golden fixtures the contract between them. That gives:

- One Maven artifact set that runs on any JVM/OS/arch — no dylib matrix, no extraction, no `java.library.path`.
- GraalVM native-image works with no JNA/reachability/resource plumbing → true single executable.
- The Rust HTML renderer remains available for Swift/.NET/cross-language projection, guarded by the same fixtures.

## Plan

**1. Port Markdown (small, ~520 LOC) — unblocks pure `pathland-view-core`**
- Replace the JNA `Markdown.java` with a pure Kotlin parser matching `pathland-markdown` semantics (bold/italic/code/strike/links and edge cases).
- Keep the `dev.pathland.markdown.Markdown` API; `isAvailable()` becomes `true`.
- Add parity tests; remove the markdown dylib embed/staging from `pathland-view-core` and release/CI.

**2. Port the HTML renderer into `lib/java/pathland-render-html` (~6k LOC)**
- Reimplement decode → retained output tree → HTML over the existing `ProtocolFrame`/`FrameCodec` (no native boundary).
- Port the supporting tables: roles, tokens, icons, typography, media shell, toggle/date modes, attributed text, proxy view, fit bands, linked/inline CSS and debug comments.
- Embed `base.css` + `base.css.name` as classpath resources from the shared synced assets (or generate a constant at build time so native-image needs no resource config).
- Keep `HtmlRenderer`'s public API identical (Kotlin `@JvmStatic`), so `PathlandSession`, Spring and Quarkus need no changes.
- Remove JNA, the antrun native embed, and platform-resolution code.

**3. Enforce parity**
- Add a JVM golden test that renders the committed `lib/typescript/test/fixtures/ssr/*.{plpl,html}` and asserts byte equality (mirrors the TS conformance test).
- Keep `pathland-html-golden` as fixture producer; CI runs Rust check + TS conformance + JVM golden. Any HTML output change updates Rust, fixtures, and Kotlin in one change.
- Drop the Java job's native-artifact handoff, the release native staging for the jars, and the Rust stage in the Quarkus `Dockerfile`.

**4. Prove the payoff**

- Add a Quarkus native CI job (`-Pnative`) verifying SSR + `/ws` + base CSS + icons in the native executable.

**Tradeoff to accept:** two HTML implementations (Rust for non-JVM, Kotlin for JVM). The golden fixtures already exist for exactly this (they currently guard Rust vs TS), so drift is testable — but every new component/property now lands in both renderers.

 # Pathland Project - AI Agent Guide
 
 This document provides essential context for AI agents (or human contributors) working on the **Pathland** protocol. It captures the project's direction, architectural decisions, and implementation details to ensure consistency.
 
 **Last Updated**: November 3, 2026
 
 ---
 
 ## Architecture: Rust Opcode Engine
 
 > The canonical core is a **Rust engine** that emits the application's
 > **declarative view structure** — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing, padding,
 > alignment — as a fixed **16-byte opcode ring buffer** into shared linear
 > memory, consumed by host renderers. View components and modifiers are written
 > in Rust with a SwiftUI-like API, and in Kotlin with the hand-written
 > **`dev.pathland.view.dsl` DSL** (reusable JVM library, Java 17+); both drive the
 > engine through the flat **native C ABI** (`pathland-view-native`) over a
 > zero-copy shared ring on desktop. Java hosts mount Kotlin views through
 > `PathlandApp`.
 
 ### The 16-byte Opcode Engine
 
 - Every opcode is exactly **16 bytes**: `Category (1B) | Command ID (1B) | Flags (2B) | A (4B) | B (4B) | C (4B)`, `#[repr(C, packed)]`, little-endian.
 - A 64-byte cache line holds exactly **4 opcodes** → L1-cache-friendly.
 - Opcodes live in a **ring buffer** in linear memory; the guest writes at `writeCursor`, the host reads from `readCursor`; frame boundaries via a monotonic `frameCount` in the header block.
 - **Both directions are binary**: a second **event ring** (host → guest) carries `EVENT`-category opcodes. The renderer writes raw inputs at `eventWriteCursor`; the guest drains them at `eventReadCursor`. Events are 16-byte opcodes through the engine, never a side-channel callback.
 - **Variable-length data** (strings, token paths) lives in a bump **arena**; opcodes reference entries by offset (`[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`), so every opcode stays 16 bytes. A second host-owned **event arena** mirrors this in the host → guest direction (shared-memory event strings, e.g. `TEXT_CHANGED`); over the network, host → guest strings ride the batch's string section.
 - **Window metadata** (`META::SET_WINDOW_METADATA`, field family `TITLE`/`DESCRIPTION`/`LOCALE`) carries the hosting surface's presentation metadata; renderers map it to their own chrome (browser `<title>`/meta description/`<html lang>`, GTK/Qt window title). It is root-scoped and signal-backed, so a route title is a computed over the router. Web-only artifacts (canonical/robots/sitemap) stay host-owned.
 - Spec: **`spec/OPCODE.md`** (primary) + **`spec/CONFORMANCE.md`** (golden vectors). Companion catalogs: **`spec/PRIMITIVES.md`** (views), **`spec/MODIFIERS.md`** (modifiers/properties), **`spec/EVENTS.md`** (events), **`spec/LAYOUT.md`** (frame & layout allocation contract) — draft IDs are allocated there spec-first.
 
 ### Declarative, not positioned (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The engine describes WHAT the UI is — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing,
 > padding, alignment — never WHERE it is. It does not compute layout and does
 > not emit rects.**
 
 - The engine emits **declarative structure** (`TREE` create/delete/insert/remove/move) + **constraint properties** (`PARAMETER` spacing/padding/alignment/FILL/HUG hints).
 - **Native elements everywhere**: each platform's renderer maps the opcode stream onto that platform's native elements — GTK4 widgets on desktop, DOM elements in the browser, HTML server-side — and those native elements lay themselves out. Never a generic canvas unless a platform has no native equivalent.
 - **Reactive emission**: emission is diff-based. Only the nodes that changed emit opcodes (property diffs via `SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_TEXT`, structural diffs via `TREE` opcodes). An unchanged tree emits **zero** opcodes. Signals in the application mark the tree dirty; the engine reconciles.
 - **Zero dynamic heap allocations** during steady-state emission (proven by test).
 
 ### no_std / wasm32 direction guard (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 `pathland-core` and `pathland-view` must remain `#![no_std]` + `alloc` and
 compile for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. This is the guarantee that the protocol
 core can still target a browser / embedded / remote projection later (goal #15,
 Quarkus SSR + WebSocket). The desktop path (`pathland-view-native`) is the only
 consumer today, but the core must not become desktop-only. Verify with
 `lib/rust/check-wasm.sh` (i.e. `cargo build -p pathland-core -p pathland-view
 --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`).
 
 ### Reactive signals (Angular-style)
 
 `pathland-core::signal` provides writable signals that live in the engine. A
 node binds its text (`Node::text_binding`), a property
 (`Node::property_bindings`) or a **string property** (`Node::string_bindings`,
 e.g. a media controller's `MEDIA_SOURCE`) to a `SignalId`; during emit the engine
 resolves the binding and records the dependency, and `Engine::set_signal`
 re-emits **only the bound nodes** (`SET_TEXT` / `SET_PROPERTY`) — no full tree
 walk. Signal values
 are one of `F32`/`U32`/`Bool`/`Enum`/`Str` (packed to the wire's `u32` value or
 arena string). Foreign hosts reach signals via the flat C ABI
 (`pathland_native_signal_create_*` / `signal_set_*` / `node_bind_text` /
 `node_bind_property`) and the Kotlin/JVM `Signal` type. Binding then calling `emit`
 records the dependency; a subsequent `set` is a partial emit. (Computed/derived
 signals + effects are the planned next step.)
 
 ### Rust Workspace (`lib/rust/`)
 
 ```
 # ── The three elements ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 crates/pathland-view/     # RETAINED UI — SwiftUI-style view DSL: VStack/HStack/Text/Button +
                           #   decoupled modifiers (spacing/padding/fontSize/color/background)
                           #   + Video (a MediaController's surface) + attach() (no_std)
 crates/pathland-core/     # PROTOCOL — 16-byte opcode, ring buffer, arena, constants, events,
                           #   memory layout, Guest/Host/Frame surface (no_std, zero-alloc).
                           #   Pure protocol; the emitter moved out to pathland-engine.
 crates/pathland-engine/   # EMITTER — retained tree types (Node/Component) + the diff-based
                           #   reactive emitter + signals + MediaController (spec/MEDIA.md).
 crates/pathland-core-transport/ # TRANSPORT — shared-memory ring owner (RingTransport) +
                           #   network batch encode/decode + batching policy (std)
 crates/pathland-render-core/ # RENDERER CORE (shared, toolkit-free) — opcode-frame decode into a
                           #   native-element description (RenderTree/HostNode), design-token
                           #   tables + resolution, concrete Tier-1 defaults. No GTK/Qt: every
                           #   renderer shares one tested decode path.
 crates/pathland-render-gtk/ # RENDERER — maps opcode frames onto native GTK widgets
                           #   incrementally; the only crate that touches GTK/glib/pango.
                           #   Fixed-size images scale to the logical-points box (gdk-pixbuf,
                           #   CONTENT_MODE fit/fill). App-driven media via a direct GStreamer
                           #   playbin (GTK4's own media backend is compiled out of some
                           #   builds). Exposes pathland_gtk_run[_ring]/

                           #   shared decode core + a sent-state delta diff + the Pump/C ABI;
                           #   a thin C++ layer (src/qt/, built via cc + moc) owns the Qt shell
                           #   and applies the delta command batch to QML items (incl. media via
                           #   QtMultimedia). The crate needs Qt6 dev libs (Homebrew: qtbase
                           #   qtdeclarative qtmultimedia) to build/test; its headless tests use
                           #   QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen.
 crates/pathland-markdown/ # PARSER — shared inline Markdown (`no_std` + alloc) into
                           #   `pathland_core::AttributedString` (bold/italic/code/strike/links).
-crates/pathland-markdown-capi/ # C ABI (cdylib `libpathland_markdown`) for Java/JNA.
+crates/pathland-markdown-capi/ # C ABI (cdylib `libpathland_markdown`) for non-JVM hosts
+                          #   (the JVM uses the pure-Java parser in pathland-view-core).
 crates/pathland-render-html/ # RENDERER — maps opcode frames onto declarative HTML (flex
 #   stacks, spans, buttons) as a pure function of the stream; the
                            #   server-side/remote-projection target (Goal #15).
 # ── Web client (DOM renderer, lib/typescript) ──────────────────────────────
 lib/typescript/                        # DOM RENDERER — @pathland/dom-renderer: a small
 ```

 ### HTML base design (`design/`)
 
 The HTML renderer's built-in stylesheet is generated from a **three-layer Style
 Dictionary pipeline** plus hand-authored reset/component CSS (one built-in base
 design; no app-facing base-design selection):
 
 ```
 design/tokens/base/*.tokens.json      # internal palette + scales (not emitted)
 design/tokens/semantic/*.tokens.json  # protocol catalog semantics (emitted)
 design/tokens/component/*.tokens.json # per-component surface (emitted)
 design/html/{reset,components}.css    # hand-authored CSS consuming var(--pl-*)
 design/scripts/{build,dev,check}.mjs  # SD build, watcher/preview, validation
 design/build/base.css                 # generated: reset + tokens + components
 design/build/base.css.name            # content hash: base-<sha256-12>.css
 ```
 
 - Tokens are flat DTCG entries (`$value`/`$type`/`$extensions.pathland`) because
   the catalog has both leaf and group paths (`control.border` vs
   `control.border.width`). Dark values live on `$extensions.pathland.dark`;
   durations/z-index/`em` icon sizes are marked internal.
 - `npm --prefix design run build` generates
   `design/build/{tokens.css,manifest.json,base.css,base.css.name}`;
   `npm --prefix design run check` validates catalog coverage, layer direction,
   dark/forced-dark declarations, dimension/`isLengthToken` rules, and the CSS
   content hash.
 - `scripts/sync-design-css.sh` copies the bundle + name to
   `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/assets/` (committed; `--check` fails on
   drift). `css.rs` embeds both with `include_str!` (`builtin_css()` /
   `builtin_css_name()`).
 - The renderer's library default is inline (`render_document`); the linked mode
   (`render_document_linked`, C ABI `pathland_html_render_linked` +
   `pathland_html_base_css[_name]`, Java `renderLinked`/`baseCss`/`baseCssName`)
   emits `{base}/base-<hash>.css`. The Spring Boot and Quarkus starters use it
   and serve the renderer-owned bytes immutable (global + mounted bases); token
   overrides/fit rules stay inline.
 - `scripts/lib.sh` (`build_rust_html`), the Maven `refresh-ide` profile, and CI
   run the design build + sync. Do not edit generated CSS by hand.
 
 ### Native C-ABI shim (`pathland-view-native` + `pathland-core-capi`)
 
 The **desktop/cross-language zero-copy path**: `pathland-view-native` exposes the
 flat world (the flat `builder`/`engine` surface) as `pathland_native_*` C
 functions with a **shared-memory ring** the host driver reads in place. Any
 language that links the dylib (Swift/Java via FFI) calls the flat surface —
 no per-component wrappers — and consumes opcodes zero-copy.
 
 `pathland-core-capi` (`libpathland_core`) is the **minimal ring C ABI** for the
 Kotlin DSL: `pathland_core_create`/`destroy`, `pathland_ring_buffer_push` (one
 raw 16-byte opcode), `pathland_core_arena_alloc`, frame boundaries, zero-copy
 `ring_ptr`/`ring_len`, and event drain/send. The Kotlin DSL
 (`dev.pathland.view.core.ffm`) binds it with **JNA** (lazily loaded, zero JNI) and
 owns the retained tree + diff emission itself.
 
 ### GTK4 Renderer (`pathland-render-gtk`)
 
 The desktop renderer: a single crate that owns **all** GTK/glib/pango usage and
 maps opcode frames **incrementally** onto native GTK widgets (a retained
 `id → gtk::Widget` map). Both the Rust demo and the Java demo render through
 it — the demos **never call GTK or Swing directly**:
 
 - Rust demo links `pathland-render-gtk` as an `rlib` and calls `GtkRenderer::run(...)`
   with a wake closure.
 - The Java/Kotlin desktop demo (`pathland-desktop-demo`) loads `pathland-render-gtk`
   as a `cdylib` via JNA and
   calls `pathland_gtk_run_ring(ring, on_event, width, height)` over the Kotlin view's
   `libpathland_core` ring; native inputs round-trip as `EVENT` opcodes through the shared
   ring. The renderer **writes** the events and **wakes** the host (no payload); the host
   drains the event ring itself via `pathland_core_drain_events`. Events are never
   delivered through a side-channel callback — they flow through the opcode engine.
   The demo mounts the Kotlin `MusicPlayerView` (the same shared view the web demos use) with the
   app-driven media contract: the renderer plays the tracks through a direct GStreamer
   `playbin` and reports `MEDIA_*` events back; the demo's web-style
   `/_pathland/assets/...` paths resolve against an extracted local asset root
   (`pathland_gtk_set_asset_root`).
 
 The renderer maps native inputs onto the raw `Event` surface via GTK4
 controllers (`Button::clicked` → pointer up, `EventControllerMotion` →
 pointer move/enter/leave), emitting events through the same `Pump::send_input`
 path.
 
 `pathland_gtk::run` passes an explicit empty argv to GTK (the process command
 line belongs to the embedding host — e.g. the JVM's `-cp`/`-D` flags — and must
 not be parsed as GTK options).
 
 ### Kotlin JVM authoring DSL (`dev.pathland.view.dsl`, in `lib/java/pathland-view-core`)
 
 The **sole JVM authoring surface**. It is the SwiftUI-like DSL shared by desktop,
 Spring Boot, Quarkus, and web apps. Components and modifiers:
 
 - `View` is an **open Kotlin interface** — the library ships `Text`/`Image`/`Color`/
   `Rectangle`, `VStack`/`HStack`/`ZStack`, `Spacer`, `Button`,
   `TextField(placeholder, WritableSignal<String>)`, `Video` (a
   `MediaController`'s surface), and application code defines its own views by
   extending `Component` or implementing `View`. **Media is a state object, not a
   view** (spec/MEDIA.md): `MediaController` owns the resource + transport as
   signals, a `Video` surface renders it, and **audio has no view** — the app
   binds its own buttons/sliders (`controller.attach()` materializes the
   controller's node once, outside any swapping branch).
 - **SwiftUI-style `body()` / reactive components**: composite views declare
   `View body()`; a signal read there subscribes that component, and a later write
   re-renders only that component and diffs its retained subtree. A signal bound
   to a node stays fine-grained and does not re-run the body. Plain
   `if`/`when`/`for` works; `ForEach` is the reactive list component.
 - **Builders and modifiers**: `VStack(spacing = 8f) { … }`, `Text("hi")`,
   `Button("Save") { … }`, `.padding`, `.frame`, `.fontSize`, `.background`,
   `.buttonStyle(BorderedButtonStyle)`, `.windowMetadata`, navigation intents, and
   the full modifier vocabulary. Styles are Kotlin values
   (`PlainButtonStyle`, `BorderedButtonStyle`, label styles, `NativeVideoStyle`).
 - **Builder scopes**: view blocks take a `PathlandScope` receiver. `PathlandScope`,
   `Navigation.Builder`, and modifier/style `Config` receivers share the
   `@PathlandDsl` marker, so an outer router/config receiver cannot be captured
   implicitly inside a nested view block (compile-time guard only; the
   thread-local `ViewScopes` stack still collects children).
 - **Persisted state**: `Component` provides `val count by state(0)` (auto-keyed
   by property name) or `state(0, "key")`, bound to the session's
   `PersistentState` before the first `body()` render — no annotation processor or
   kapt.
 - **Java hosting**: Java Spring Boot/Quarkus apps remain first-class hosts. A
   Java `PathlandApp` bean returns a Kotlin `View`
   (`return () -> MusicPlayerView.make();`); no Kotlin compiler or authoring DSL is
   needed in the host module. Every reusable Kotlin root exposes a public
   constructor or `@JvmStatic make(...)` factory with Java-friendly types.
 - **Consistency** with `pathland_core::constants` is enforced by the
   emitter/HTML tests (golden byte layout + round-trips).

 ## Project Vision
 
 **Pathland is a cross-platform, cross-language UI protocol** that enables retained-mode UI development with multiple renderer backends. It is **protocol-first**, meaning the protocol specification is the source of truth, not any particular implementation.
 
 **Primary Goal**: Write once, run anywhere - Enable UI code to be written once and deployed across web, mobile, desktop, and embedded platforms through different renderer implementations.
 
 **Status**: The Rust opcode engine (16-byte opcode, ring buffer, arena, diff-based reactive emission) is implemented and tested (`cargo test`). See the Architecture section above.
 
 ---
 
 ## CRITICAL ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES
 
 ### Principle 1: Renderer Statelessness (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The renderer MUST NOT retain application state.**
 
 - Renderers are **pure functions** of the opcode stream: same opcodes → same output
 - A renderer MAY retain its **rendered-output tree** (id → native element + computed layout) for drawing, hit-testing, and event routing — this is a cache of its own output, not state
 - The renderer MUST NOT retain component property values as business state, application control flow, or anything the application can change without emitting an opcode
 - The application owns the canonical retained UI tree
 - The engine emits **deltas only**; the renderer applies them to its native elements
 
 **Violation of this principle is a bug, not a feature.**
 
 ### Principle 2: Command-Based Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol transmits tree mutations as a stream of commands, NOT as serialized trees.**
 
 - Each frame is a **batch of delta commands** describing changes
 - Only **actual changes** are transmitted (diff-based reactive emission)
 - Protocol acts like a **VM instruction stream** / ABI
 - Deterministic, linear decoding without schema lookup or reflection
 
 ### Principle 3: Binary Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol MUST be binary.**
 
 - Open-source, cross-platform binary format
 - Fixed **16-byte instructions** in a ring buffer shared with the host via linear memory
 - Custom instruction-based bytecode, not schema-driven serialization
 - **Both directions are binary**: tree mutations (app → renderer) AND raw-input events (renderer → app) share the same instruction format, so the wire is language- and platform-agnostic

 ### Opcode Format
 
 Every opcode is exactly 16 bytes:
 
 ```
 [Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]
 ```
 
 See `spec/OPCODE.md` for the full format, ring buffer, arena, and frame lifecycle.
 
 ### Machine-readable protocol manifest
 
 `spec/protocol.tsv` is the target-neutral ID manifest emitted from
 `pathland_core::constants` by `pathland-protocol-manifest` (`cargo run -p
 pathland-protocol-manifest`). It contains only `kind`, `group`, `name`, and
 `value`; each language binding keeps its own representation and validates or
 reads the manifest. There is no Rust→JVM source generation.
 
 The JVM mirror is hand-written and checked by
 `pathland-view-core/src/test/java/.../ProtocolManifestTest`: every manifest row
 must match a Java constant, no extra public numeric constants may exist, and
 `ValueTypes.forProperty` must match `property_value_type`. CI regenerates the
 manifest from Rust and fails on drift.
 
 Engine behavior beyond individual opcodes is specified in `spec/ENGINE.md` and
 enforced by shared self-contained frame traces under `spec/engine-traces/`.
 `pathland-engine-golden` emits them from the Rust engine and the JVM
 `EngineTraceTest` compares its encoded frames byte-for-byte.
 
 ### Categories
 
 | Category | Value | Direction | Description |
 |----------|-------|-----------|-------------|
 | TREE | 0x01 | Guest → Host | Node create/delete/insert/remove/move |
 | PARAMETER | 0x02 | Guest → Host | Constraint properties (spacing, padding, …), design tokens |
 | EVENT | 0x03 | Host → Guest | Raw inputs: pointer down/move/up, key down/up |
 | META | 0x04 | Both | Reset, environment, window metadata |

 ### Key Property IDs
 
 **Stack**: SPACING=0x0001, ALIGNMENT=0x0002, CONTENT_MARGINS=0x0005  
 **Text**: TEXT=0x000A, TEXT_ALIGNMENT=0x000C, LINE_LIMIT=0x000B, TRUNCATION_MODE=0x000D

 ### Colors
 
 - Literal colors are **sRGB** with D65 white point, packed as `0xAARRGGBB`
 - A color property may instead carry a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference to a token path
 - Semantic token resolution and theme adaptation are **renderer-owned**
 
 ### Design Token System
 
 **Core Principle**: Application defines intent, overrides, and the theme.
 Renderer defines visual appearance, behavior, defaults, and interaction states.
 
 - The **application owns the theme**: token overrides (base = **light**, `dark.`-prefixed = **dark**) and token references in style properties. Token refs cover COLOR and non-color values (`Length` for spacing/padding/font size/radius/border/frame; `FontFamily.Token` for STRING) in the Rust and Kotlin DSLs.
 - The **renderer owns** default token values (light + dark, the full Tier-1 catalog), token resolution (including explicit `dark.` = forced dark and parent fallback), effective color-scheme detection, interaction states (hover, pressed, focus, disabled), and theme adaptation
 - `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` identifies tokens by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`) with the standard value-type encoding — there is no separate numeric tokenId system. A `dark.` prefix selects the dark variant (`dark.color.primary`); a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference whose path starts with `dark.` forces the dark value in either scheme
 - **Runtime theming**: `META::RESET_THEME` clears every app override; a replacement theme is reset + `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides in one frame. `META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME` forces `platform`/`light`/`dark`. Both are renderer state — no node is re-emitted. Java: `Emitter.replaceTheme`/`setColorScheme` + `PathlandSession.setTheme`/`setColorScheme`; Rust: `Engine::reset_theme`/`set_color_scheme`.
 - An unresolvable token reference leaves the property **unset** (renderer default), never an error or stale value.
 - The protocol MUST NEVER describe hover styles, click styles, visual transitions, conditional styling, or layout tuning for interaction states
 - **Deferred**: applying per-component tokens to native GTK/Qt leaf control chrome; web parent-path fallback.
 
 The HTML renderer's default token values are generated from `design/` (see
 "HTML base design" above). Full details: [Design Token System](./spec/OPCODE.md#design-token-system)
 and the canonical catalog / color-scheme contract in [spec/TOKENS.md](./spec/TOKENS.md).

 ## Implementation Guidelines
 
 ### Adding New Component
 1. Add to `component_type` in `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/src/constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Implement the component type in `pathland-core` (if it affects the retained tree)
 4. Implement native-element mapping in the target renderer (Goal 3–5)
 5. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Adding New Property
 1. Add to the appropriate property module in `constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Handle the value type in `pathland-core`'s diff emission (if a stack/text/size property)
 4. Implement in each renderer's property application
 5. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Modifying Protocol
 1. Update `spec/OPCODE.md` first (and `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` vectors)
 2. Update `constants.rs` and `pathland-core` encoding/emitters
 3. Run `cd lib/rust && cargo run -p pathland-protocol-manifest` and commit the
    updated `spec/protocol.tsv`
 4. Update the hand-written JVM protocol constants (the Java manifest test fails

 ### NEVER Do These

 ## Pathland Mindset
 
 **Always remember**:
 1. Protocol is King
 2. Renderers are Dumb (execute commands only)
 3. Applications are Smart (generate commands)
 4. Only Changes Matter (transmit mutations / reactive emission)
 5. Binary is Beautiful (efficient, deterministic)
 
 **When in doubt**: Check `spec/OPCODE.md`, the conformance vectors in `spec/CONFORMANCE.md`, and the companion catalogs (`spec/PRIMITIVES.md`, `spec/MODIFIERS.md`, `spec/EVENTS.md`, `spec/LAYOUT.md`), and the reference implementation (`pathland-core`). [![CI](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml) ## Pathland is a protocol Pathland is first and foremost a **binary UI protocol** — not just a framework, and not a single rendering target. Your view declaration compiles to fixed 16-byte opcodes that any renderer applies to native elements. The wire is the contract: a view written in Kotlin, Rust, or any other supported DSL produces the **same opcode stream**, and any renderer can apply it. That makes Pathland **language- and renderer-agnostic**: - **Write the UI once, declaratively.** A SwiftUI-shaped DSL in your language of choice — Kotlin, Rust, anything — describes the same view structure, whatever it later runs on. - **Run it on any surface.** The same view code drives today's server-rendered web and the native GTK4 desktop renderer, and is on track for the browser via WASM, embedded chips (LVGL), and native mobile/desktop (SwiftUI/UIKit, Jetpack Compose, Qt) ([Where it's headed](#where-its-headed)). - **Only changes travel.** The protocol is a stream of tiny binary deltas: an unchanged screen transmits zero bytes, and updates are applied in place. **Server-side rendering is the first surface we ship** — the flagship getting-started path — **not the whole story**. It's the on-ramp that's useful today; the protocol underneath is where the portability comes from. ## See it in action The same shared demo views, rendered by two of Pathland's surfaces — server-side HTML in the browser and native GTK4 widgets on the desktop:

Browser — SSR + live WebSocket deltas
Desktop — native GTK4 renderer
Try the hosted Quarkus demo live: **[pathland.onrender.com](https://pathland.onrender.com)**. ## The flagship path today: SSR The fastest way to replace a BFF + JavaScript-frontend stack. You write the **whole UI in your backend language** — Kotlin, Rust, anything. Pathland renders the first page as server-side HTML, so it appears instantly, then keeps it alive with tiny binary updates over a WebSocket. The result is a smooth, reactive UI — delivered by the backend team, without npm, bundlers, an extra build pipeline, or a separate frontend. ``` You declare the UI in your backend │ ▼ The server renders it (HTML) and owns it │ ▼ Only the things that change travel to the client │ ▼ The client applies them to native elements (60FPS) ``` - **You declare the UI** with a SwiftUI-shaped DSL — `VStack`, `Text`, `Button`, styling — right next to your business logic. - **The server renders and owns it.** The first page is plain HTML (instant paint, SEO-friendly); the server keeps the authoritative copy of the UI. - **Only changes travel.** A click, a signal update, a navigation — the server sends a few tiny binary bytes describing exactly what changed. An unchanged screen sends nothing. The client applies them to real native elements (browser DOM, GTK widgets), so the platform does the layout, animation, and accessibility. ## The whole app Add one dependency and one bean, and you have a working app. **Spring Boot** ```java @SpringBootApplication public class MyApp { public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args); } @Bean PathlandApp pathlandApp() { return () -> new MyHomeView(); } } ``` **Quarkus** ```java @ApplicationScoped public class MyApp implements PathlandApp { public View newRoot() { return new MyHomeView(); } } ``` `MyHomeView` is a Kotlin view — authored once and mounted by any JVM host: ```kotlin class MyHomeView : Component() { private var count by state(0) // persisted per session, automatically override fun body(): View = VStack(alignment = HorizontalAlignment.CENTER, spacing = 8f) { Text(computed { "Clicked $count times" }) Button("Click me") { count += 1 } }.padding(24f) } ``` A Java Spring Boot or Quarkus app mounts it without any Kotlin authoring code: ```java @Bean PathlandApp pathlandApp() { return () -> new MyHomeView(); } ``` That's it — SSR at any path, live updates over `/ws`, per-session state. *(Imports omitted: the Kotlin view DSL lives in `dev.pathland.view.dsl`; Java hosts only need `dev.pathland.server.PathlandApp` and a Kotlin view factory.)* ## What it removes Today's server team pays for a BFF, a client-side state model, a SPA framework, and a JS build toolchain — all to render UI the server already owns. Pathland removes that layer: the backend *is* the application. There is no frontend contract to maintain, no client state model, and no JavaScript to write — and the same backend code that serves the web can drive other renderers later. ## Why it's smooth Pathland is built for smooth 60FPS UIs: - **Only changes are sent.** A screen that isn't changing transmits zero bytes. Updates are tiny binary deltas, not re-rendered pages or JSON trees. - **Native elements, not a canvas.** The platform lays out and animates real elements — you get native layout, text rendering, and accessibility for free, whether those elements are DOM nodes or GTK widgets. - **A thin client.** The web client is a small static file that hydrates the server HTML and applies updates in place. No framework, no virtual DOM, no re-render cost. ## The part you don't write The web client is a single prebuilt JavaScript file you copy into your static resources. It's shipped, not maintained — all the real logic lives in your backend. (There's also a native GTK renderer for desktop.) ## Where it runs today - **Web (SSR + live WebSocket deltas)** — Kotlin views with Java or Kotlin hosts, via the Spring Boot and Quarkus extensions and demos; the flagship getting-started path. - **Native desktop (GTK4 + Qt)** — renderers driven by the same protocol, from the Rust DSL and the shared Kotlin `MusicPlayerView` (`pathland-desktop-demo`). Two surfaces, one protocol — the demos' shared views run under both without a rewrite. ## Where it's headed The SSR path above is the on-ramp — the protocol isn't limited to it. Write the app logic once, run it on embedded, mobile, desktop, and browser. Pathland is an open protocol, so the same code that drives the server-rendered UI today can also run on the device itself: - **In the browser**, the app logic compiles to WASM, writes to a shared buffer, and the main thread is left to rendering alone. - **On embedded devices**, the logic runs on one core while another core renders, with the ring buffer carrying the protocol between them — mapped onto a lightweight UI toolkit like LVGL. - **On mobile and desktop**, the same logic drives native renderers — SwiftUI/UIKit on Apple platforms, Jetpack Compose on Android, Qt and GTK on desktop.  # Releasing Pathland
 
 Publishing a **GitHub Release** (tagged `vX.Y.Z`) runs
 `.github/workflows/release.yml`, which sets the version from the tag, builds and
 publishes every artifact, attaches the built files to the Release, and commits
 the version back to `main`:
 
 | Ecosystem | Artifacts | Registry |
 |-----------|-----------|----------|
 | Rust | `pathland-core`, `pathland-markdown`, `pathland-engine`, `pathland-view`, `pathland-core-transport`, `pathland-render-html` | crates.io |
 | Java | `dev.pathland:*` libraries (incl. the renderer + view-core native libs for windows-x86_64, linux-x86_64, linux-aarch64, macos-aarch64) | Maven Central |
 
 ## Versioning (tag-driven)
 
 **The tag drives the version** — no pre-bump commit is needed:
 
 - The workflow writes `X.Y.Z` (from the tag `vX.Y.Z`) into
   `lib/rust/Cargo.toml` (`[workspace.package] version` + the intra-workspace
   path-dep pins, via `cargo set-version --workspace`) and
   `lib/java/pom.xml` (via `mvn versions:set`) **in CI**, then publishes.
 - A `bump` job then commits that version back to `main`, so `main` always
   reflects the latest release.
 
 Tags must be `v<major>.<minor>.<patch>` (an optional pre-release suffix is
 allowed); the `version` job fails on anything else. Releases are immutable per
 version — pick a new tag to re-release.
 
 ## One-time setup
 
 Repository secrets (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions):
 
 - `CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN` — a crates.io API token with publish scope
   (https://crates.io/settings/tokens).
 - `GPG_PRIVATE_KEY` — an armored GPG private key whose public key is on a
   keyserver (Central verifies the signatures).
 - `GPG_PASSPHRASE` — that key's passphrase.
 - `CENTRAL_USERNAME` / `CENTRAL_PASSWORD` — a Sonatype Central Portal **user
   token** (https://central.sonatype.com/account).
 
 Also: `main` must be pushable by the workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN` (the `bump` job).
 If `main` is protected, allow the Actions bot, or the bump step fails (after a
 successful publish).
 
 ## Release
 
 1. Create a **GitHub Release** on `main` tagged `vX.Y.Z` (publish it).
 2. The workflow runs:
    - `version` — derive + validate `X.Y.Z` from the tag.
    - `rust` — set the version, test the publishable crates, publish them to
      crates.io in dependency order, upload the `.crate` files.
-   - `java-natives` — build `libpathland_render_html` and
-     `libpathland_markdown` for windows-x86_64, linux-x86_64, linux-aarch64,
-     macos-aarch64.
+   - `java-natives` — build `libpathland_render_html` for windows-x86_64,
+     linux-x86_64, linux-aarch64, macos-aarch64. (The JVM Markdown parser is
+     pure Java, so no markdown native is staged for the jars.)
     - `java` — set the version, stage the natives into the renderer jar, run
       `mvn -P release deploy` to Maven Central (auto-published after validation).
     - `bump` — commit the version back to `main`.
     - `release-assets` — attach the `.crate` files, the Java main jars, and the
       native libs to the GitHub Release.
 
 The Java deploy runs on **Maven 3.9.9** (pinned in the workflow): Maven 3.10
 writes a `maven-metadata-local.xml` beside each artifact in the Central staging,
 which the Portal rejects ("content that does NOT have a .pom file"). The demos
 are **excluded from the release reactor** (`-pl '!pathland-demo-views-kotlin,!pathland-desktop-demo,!pathland-quarkus-demo,!pathland-spring-boot-demo'`)
 — `central-publishing-maven-plugin` bundles every reactor module, ignoring
 `maven.deploy.skip`, and the demos must not be published.
 
 The publish steps are **idempotent**: a crate+version already on crates.io is
 skipped, so re-running a partially failed release is safe (re-run the workflow
 via `workflow_dispatch`, passing the `tag`). Maven Central rejects a re-deploy of
 an existing version, so a Java re-run only helps if the Java deploy did not
 complete.
 
 ## Local pre-flight
 
 Rust — `cargo publish --dry-run -p pathland-core` validates the leaf crate (the
 dependent crates can only be dry-run once their dependencies are on crates.io,
 so the ordered CI publish validates them).
 
 Java — `mvn -P release verify` builds and signs the sources/javadoc jars without
 uploading. It needs GPG installed and a `central` server in `~/.m2/settings.xml`:
 
 ```xml
 <server>
   <id>central</id>
   <username>TOKEN_USERNAME</username>
   <password>TOKEN_PASSWORD</password>
 </server>
 ```
 
 ## Publishable crates (dependency order)
 
 ```
 pathland-core → pathland-markdown → pathland-engine → pathland-view → pathland-core-transport → pathland-render-html
 ```
 
 (`pathland-view-native`, `pathland-core-capi`, `pathland-markdown-capi`,
 `pathland-render-gtk`, `pathland-render-gtk-demo`, `pathland-html-golden`,
 `pathland-ts-codegen` are **not** published — C-ABI cdylibs, the GTK renderer,
 and dev tools.)
 
 ## Published Java modules
 
 `pathland-view-core` (Kotlin JVM engine/SPI + the sole authoring DSL),
 `pathland-render-html`, `pathland-server-core` (runtime, telemetry adapters,
 Redis state store, and the shared WS test harness), `pathland-spring-boot-starter`,
 `pathland-quarkus`, `pathland-quarkus-deployment` (plus the `pathland-parent`
 POM). The demo modules (`pathland-demo-views-kotlin`, `pathland-desktop-demo`,
 `pathland-quarkus-demo`, `pathland-spring-boot-demo`) set `maven.deploy.skip`.

+Markdown parser is pure Java and needs no native build.
 
 The image's Maven step selects both `pathland-quarkus-demo` and
 `pathland-quarkus-deployment`. The deployment module is not a Maven dependency of
 the demo, but the runtime extension descriptor validates its dependencies against
 it; omitting it makes a fresh (empty `~/.m2`) build fail Quarkus extension
 verification.
 
 ## Run locally
 
 ```bash
 docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 pathland-quarkus-demo
 # → http://localhost:8080
 ```
 
 A quick check that it serves:
 
 ```bash
 curl -I http://localhost:8080/          # 200, text/html
 curl http://localhost:8080/ | grep -o 'data-pathland-id'   # hydrated SSR markup
 ```
 
 State defaults to the in-memory store (no Redis needed for the demo). To use
 Redis, pass a `REDIS_URL` and the Redis `StateStore` in `pathland-server-core` is
 selected at runtime — the standalone demo runs without it.
 
 ## Push to a registry
 
 ```bash
 docker tag pathland-quarkus-demo ghcr.io/<org>/pathland-quarkus-demo:latest
 docker push ghcr.io/<org>/pathland-quarkus-demo:latest
 ```
 
 ## Deploy to a host
 
 Any platform that runs a Docker container exposing TCP 8080 works:
 
 - **Railway / Fly.io** — point at the image (or use a Dockerfile deploy); set the
   public port to **8080**. The app binds `0.0.0.0` (see
   `application.properties`).
 - **Hetzner / any VPS** — `docker run -d -p 8080:8080 --name pathland pathland-quarkus-demo`
   (optionally behind Caddy/nginx; forward `GET /` and the WebSocket `Upgrade`).
 - **Platform port override** — the app honors `QUARKUS_HTTP_PORT` if a platform
   assigns a different port.
 
 ### Requirements
 
 - **WebSocket support**: the demo keeps the first page live via `/ws` (raw-input
   events + `PLPL` deltas). The reverse proxy / load balancer must forward the
   WebSocket `Upgrade` headers; most PaaS do this by default.
 - **Health check**: `GET /` returning 200 with HTML is the simplest probe. The
   container has no separate health endpoint.
 - **Memory**: the JVM is capped at 256 MB (`-Xmx256m`); the demo is small.

 # pathland-view-core (JVM engine + DSL) — implementation status
 
 **Last updated:** November 5, 2026
 
 The shared, framework-agnostic JVM engine, runtime and authoring DSL for the
 Pathland protocol, written entirely in Kotlin. It owns the `View` SPI and shared
 authoring vocabulary, the retained-tree diff emitter,
 signals/computed/effects, the wire codec, router, cross-platform state, JNA ring
 interop, and the `dev.pathland.view.dsl` SwiftUI-shaped builders/modifiers.
 Server and renderer modules depend on this one module; Java hosts consume the
 Kotlin-authored views through JVM interop.
 
 ## Implemented
 
 - **Protocol** (`dev.pathland.view.core.protocol`): `Components`, `Properties`,
   `Commands` (incl. `SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT`), `Categories`, `ValueTypes`, `Opcode`,
   `ValueEncoder`, `WireValue`, `TokenPath`.
 - **Attributed text** (`dev.pathland.view.core.AttributedString`): pure-Kotlin
   model + range-tracking builder (Kotlin char indices → UTF-8 byte offsets) and
   payload encode/decode; `Text(AttributedString)` / `Text(Signal<AttributedString>)`
   emit `SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT` through the emitter and both sinks.
 - **Built-in inline Markdown**: `Text("...")` parses the v1 subset by default
   (`**bold**`/`__bold__`, `*italic*`/`_italic_`, `` `code` ``,
   `~~strikethrough~~`, `[label](url)`); `markdown = false` renders literal text.
-  The shared Rust parser (`libpathland_markdown`) is embedded in the view-core
-  jar and called through `dev.pathland.markdown.Markdown` (pre-scan + bounded
-  cache). Plain results use the compact `SET_TEXT` path; rich results emit
+  `dev.pathland.markdown.Markdown` is now a **pure-Java parser** (no native
+  library, so it runs on every platform and under GraalVM native-image); it is a
+  behavioural port of the Rust `pathland-markdown` crate (pre-scan + bounded
+  cache). The Rust crate remains the parser for the Rust DSL and non-JVM hosts.
+  Plain results use the compact `SET_TEXT` path; rich results emit
   `SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT`. Reactive `Text(Signal<String>)` parses on change.
 - **Signals** (`dev.pathland.view.core.signal`): `signal`/`state`/`computed`/
   `effect`/`untracked`, synchronous glitch-free flush, equality suppression, error
   caching/retry, circular-dependency detection, and a thread-safe global
   `Scheduler`. `Signals.state` binds to the ambient session `PersistentState`
   during a component render.
 - **State** (`dev.pathland.view.core.state`): `PersistentState`, untyped
   `StateStore`, in-memory store and provider. Kotlin `Component` state delegates
   bind directly before `body()`; the Java `State` field/binder machinery and
   annotation processor are removed.
 - **Transport** (`dev.pathland.view.core.transport`): `ProtocolFrame`,
   `FrameCodec`, `Event`, `EnvironmentData`, `OpcodeSink`, `FrameOpcodeSink`.
 - **Router** (`dev.pathland.view.core.router`): `Route`, `RouteTable`, `Router`,
   `Navigation`, `NavigationContainer`, `NavigationIntent`, `Params`, `Chrome`,
   `NavOp`. `NavigationLink` and the navigation helpers live in the Kotlin DSL.
 - **JNA interop** (`dev.pathland.view.core.ffm`): lazy `PathlandCore` binding and
   `RingOpcodeSink` over `libpathland_core`.
 - **Emitter** (`dev.pathland.view.engine`): `Emitter`, `PathlandNode`, `ViewSlot`,
   `RenderResult`, `InputDispatcher`, `ReactiveValues`, `DateInput`, `MediaInput`.
   Implements mount/id assignment, diff-based reactive emission, node-level binding
   effects, structural reconciliation, fit/media/navigation routing, and the
   zero-opcode unchanged recompute contract. Registered `MediaController`s are
   projected as pinned, non-visual root children; `unregisterMediaController`
   removes them without touching the app tree.
 - **Shared SPI/values** (`dev.pathland.view.core`): `View`, `ViewModifier`,
   `Configurable`, `ChildrenView`, `Modified`, `ViewBuilder`,
   `Environment*`, `Platform`, `Theme*`, `MediaController`, `WindowMetadata`,
   `ProxyConfig`, `Color`, `Length`, shared enums, style protocols, and modifier
   wrappers.
 - **Protocol manifest validation** (`ProtocolManifestTest`): the hand-written
   protocol constants (`Components`, `Properties`, `Commands`, `Categories`,
   `ValueTypes`) are checked against `spec/protocol.tsv` — including no extra
   public numeric constants and the full `ValueTypes.forProperty` mapping. No
   Java source is generated.
 - **Shared engine traces**: the Kotlin DSL tests run the mount/text/property
   scenarios against the Rust-emitted PLPL fixtures under `spec/engine-traces/`,
   byte-for-byte. The canonical order lives in `spec/ENGINE.md`.
 - **Tests**: `pathland-view-core` owns the signal, state, frame-codec, and
   protocol-manifest tests; Kotlin DSL tests exercise the emitter end-to-end, and
   the server/HTML/desktop consumers cover their integration paths.
 
 ## Authoring DSL (`dev.pathland.view.dsl`)
 
 - **SwiftUI-shaped builders**: `Text` (plain, `Signal<String>`, or
   `AttributedString` / `Signal<AttributedString>`), `Image`, `Icon`, `Color`,
   `Rectangle`, `Circle`, `Ellipse`, `Capsule`, `RoundedRectangle`, `Shape`,
   `Divider`, `Spacer`, `ProgressView`, `Gauge`, `Label`, `Group`.
 - **Containers**: `VStack`, `HStack`, `ZStack`, `Grid`, `GridRow`, `ScrollView`,
   `LazyVStack`, `LazyHStack`, `LazyVGrid`, `LazyHGrid`, `ViewThatFits`/`Fit`,
   `ProxyView`, `ForEach`.
 - **Controls**: `Button` (title or label subtree), `TextField`, `SecureField`,
   `TextEditor`, `Toggle`, `Slider`, `Stepper`, `DatePicker`, `Picker`, `Menu`,
   `ColorPicker`.
 - **Automatic child collection**: `VStack { Text("a"); Text("b") }` needs no
   `.children(...)`. A custom `Component` constructed inline in a block
   auto-registers; a view stored as a field is added explicitly with `+field`.
 - **Scope isolation** (`@PathlandDsl`): every view builder lambda takes a
   `PathlandScope` receiver, and `PathlandScope`, `Navigation.Builder`, and the
   modifier/style `Config` receivers carry the same `@DslMarker`. An outer
   router/config receiver therefore cannot be captured implicitly inside a
   nested view builder (e.g. `fallback(...)` inside `VStack { }` is a compile
   error). Child collection itself is unchanged — the thread-local `ViewScopes`
   stack still drives auto-registration.
 - **Signals**: `signal`, `computed`, `constant`, `effect`, `untracked`,
   `Signal<T>.value`, `WritableSignal<T>.value`, `Signal<T>.map`, `readonly`.
 - **Modifier sugar**: `.padding`, `.frame`, `.offset`, `.position`, `.fixedSize`,
   layout priority/z-index/aspect ratio, the full text-formatting surface,
   foreground/background/border/corner radius/shadow, visual effects, transforms,
   visibility/disabled/hit-testing, accessibility, tap/pointer events,
   environment binding, styles, window metadata, and navigation intents.
 - **Persisted state**: `Component` base class + `val count by state(0)`
   (auto-keyed by property name) or `state(0, "key")`; a `mutableState(0)` signal
   form for two-way controls.
 - **Reactive bodies**: plain `if`/`when`/`for` in `body()`; `ForEach` over a static
   list or `Signal<List<T>>` with row-scoped child collection.
 - **Navigation**: `navigator { route(...) }`, `NavigationStack`, `NavigationLink`,
   `isActive`, and `.navigate`/`.push`/`.replace` intents.
 - **Media**: `Video(controller)` stays where the app places it; audio remains
   view-less. `controller.register()` projects a controller at the root.
 - **Naming**: the composite base is `Component` (renamed from `KotlinView` now
   that the Java DSL is gone); see #174.
 - **Java hosting**: a Java Spring Boot / Quarkus app mounts a Kotlin view through
   the Java-friendly `PathlandApp` functional interface
   (`return () -> MusicPlayerView.make();`). Kotlin roots expose public
   constructors and/or `@JvmStatic make(...)` factories.
 
 ## Package boundary
 
 - `pathland-view-core` is one Maven module: `core`/`engine`/`dsl` are logical
   subpackages inside it, with a few deliberate intra-module references
   (`Color`/`MediaController`/`Modified` materialize `PathlandNode`). Splitting
   them into separate artifacts would require a node SPI first.
 - Production runtimes/renderers (`pathland-server-core`,
   `pathland-render-html`) depend on this module. Framework starters remain
   DSL-neutral at compile time; they mount Kotlin-authored fixture views in test
   scope.
